title: No One Knows the State-of-the-Art in Geospatial Foundation Models
claim: Evaluation practice is fragmented: most benchmarks are used by few papers, many papers share none, and this isn't converging over time.
layout: 3 panels left-to-right, bar chart, histogram, dual-axis line-bar, captions beneath
description: Three side-by-side plots with long captions below each. Panel (a) is a horizontal bar chart in dark maroon showing the top-10 of 401 benchmarks by paper count, led by EuroSAT at 42, then NWPU-RESISC45 at 36 and AID at 33, down to LEVIR-CD at 13. The title gives Gini=0.51. Panel (b) is a histogram of per-paper overlap with the field-wide top-10 benchmarks. A tall bar at zero overlap stands out, and a vertical red line marks the mean of 0.27. Panel (c) overlays a red line with markers for the Gini coefficient on light gray bars for papers per year, 2021 to 2025. The title reads 'No steady convergence'. The palette is restrained: maroon, gray and one red accent. Bold caption headers state each takeaway. The eye goes first to the long bars in (a), then to the zero-overlap spike in (b).
caption: How the 152-paper corpus uses benchmarks. Panel (a) shows the top-10 benchmarks evaluated in the corpus; panel (b) shows that 35% of papers do not test on the most-used benchmarks at all; panel (c) shows that this pattern is not improving over time. Together the three panels say no GFM in the corpus can be ranked literature-wide, because the numbers needed for a fair comparison are not reported on enough shared benchmarks.
abstract: Geospatial foundation models (GFMs) have been proposed as generalizable backbones for disaster response, land-cover mapping, food-security monitoring, and other high-stakes Earth-observation tasks. Yet the published work about these models does not give reviewers or users enough information to tell which model fits a given task. We argue that nobody knows what the current state of the art is in geospatial foundation models. The methods may be useful, but the GFM literature does not standardize evaluations, training and testing protocols, released weights, or pretraining controls well enough for anyone to compare or rank them. In a 152-paper audit, we find 47 cross-paper disagreements of at least 5 percentage points, including 18 of at least 10 points, within model, benchmark, and protocol groups; 94/126 papers with pretraining data use a configuration no other paper uses; and 39% of GFM papers release no model weights. This lack of community standards can be solved. We propose six concrete expectations: named-license weight release, shared core evaluations, copied-versus-rerun baseline annotations, variance reporting, one shared evaluation harness, and data-vs-architecture-vs-algorithm controls. These gaps are a coordination failure, not a fault of any individual lab; the authors of this paper, like many others in the GFM community, have contributed to them. Rather than just critiquing the community, we aim to provide concrete steps toward a shared understanding of how to evaluate and improve GFMs.
